title: Graph Representational Learning: When Does More Expressivity Hurt Generalization?
claim: Greater model expressivity does not improve generalization: mid-expressivity models fit and generalize best, while highly expressive ones overfit and degrade under noise.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, bar chart then two line plots with legends
description: Three side-by-side plots. The left panel is a horizontal grouped bar chart titled 'GNN error on cycle task'. It lists models from MPNN up to F3-, F4- and F7-MPNN, then Sub-G, L-G and LF-G. Each model has a blue train bar and a red test bar, both with error bars. Test error is high for most models, about 13–15%. F4-MPNN and F7-MPNN are the exceptions, with low test error. Train error is near zero for all models. The middle panel shows training loss on Mutagenicity against epoch. Five curves for different label-noise levels, from 0.0 to 1.0, decay at different speeds. The curves use different colors and dash styles. The right panel plots test error against noise p for three datasets: Mutagenicity, BZR and NCI109. All three rise from about 0.2 to about 0.5 as noise increases. The eye goes first to the red and blue bars on the left.
caption: Left: Train–test errors for several GNN variants on a synthetic cycle-counting task; moderately expressive models such as F4-MPNN (Barcel´o et al., 2021), i.e., MPNNs augmented with cycle counts, generalize best, while more expressive ones tend to overfit. Center: Training-loss curves of a MPNN on MUTAGENICITY under increasing label noise p. Right: Corresponding test errors on BZR, MUTAGENICITY, and NCI109 rises sharply as label-structure correlation is essential for generalization (mean ± standard deviation across five seeds). See Appendix I.1 for more details.
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are powerful tools for learning on structured data, yet the relationship between their expressivity and predictive performance remains unclear. We introduce a family of premetrics that capture different degrees of structural similarity between graphs and relate these similarities to generalization, and consequently, the performance of expressive GNNs. By considering a setting where graph labels are correlated with structural features, we derive generalization bounds that depend on the distance between training and test graphs, model complexity, and training set size. These bounds reveal that more expressive GNNs may generalize worse unless their increased complexity is balanced by a sufficiently large training set or reduced distance between training and test graphs. Our findings relate expressivity and generalization, offering theoretical insights supported by empirical results.
